coursesExamined.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
coursesExamined.name: Personal & Professional Development
coursesExamined.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
coursesExamined.discipline: Academic writing
coursesExamined.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
coursesExamined.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

coursesExamined.description2: You will learn how to function in a ‘real-world’ design and development team for consumer products. We go through the phases of design and development: probe customer needs, translate these into a product concept, develop a fabrication method, analyze sustainability, analyze costs and proceeds. Design and development involves interviewing customers, brainstorming, laboratory experiments, quantitative modeling, constructing a prototype, and considering protection of intellectual property.
coursesExamined.name: Consumer Product Design
coursesExamined.profile: Teaches consumer-product design and development through projects that progress from understanding an existing product to creating a new one. Students investigate product mechanisms and environmental impact, interview potential customers, translate needs into specifications, select concepts, and develop production plans and prototypes where feasible. The final project integrates these stages with industrial scaling and elementary economic analysis. Sustainability, including material use, repairability, lifespan and circularity, informs design decisions throughout.
coursesExamined.discipline: Product design; Product and process development; Sustainable design
coursesExamined.topics: Consumer needs; Product concepts and specifications; Product working mechanisms; Prototyping; Laboratory-to-industrial production scaling; Materials and resource use; Product lifespan, repairability and circularity; Environmental impact; Production costs and commercial viability
coursesExamined.methods: Consumer interviews; Needs ranking and specification development; Concept-criteria matrices; Quantitative product modelling; Product investigation and experimentation; Prototyping; Process-flow diagrams and material balances; Environmental-impact estimation; Break-even analysis

coursesExamined.description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
coursesExamined.name: Optimization Methods in AI
coursesExamined.profile: Studies search and optimization for rational agents in known, complex and adversarial environments. Students move from uninformed and heuristic search to local and global optimization, first- and second-order methods and population approaches. Adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimization extend the toolkit. Laboratories and projects require algorithm tracing, implementation and evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
coursesExamined.discipline: Artificial intelligence; Mathematical optimization; Computer science
coursesExamined.topics: Intelligent and rational agents; Uninformed and informed search; Heuristic functions; Search in complex environments; Local and global optimization; First- and second-order optimization; Population methods; Adversarial games; Constraint satisfaction; Linear programming; Discrete optimization
coursesExamined.methods: Uninformed and heuristic search; Local and global search; First- and second-order optimization; Population-based optimization; Adversarial search; Monte Carlo tree search; Constraint-satisfaction algorithms; Linear programming; Discrete optimization; Algorithm implementation and experimental evaluation

coursesExamined.description2: Teaches design and analysis of algorithms and data structures, emphasizing performance analysis and focusing on prominent algorithms and data structures.
coursesExamined.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
coursesExamined.profile: Studies algorithm design and analysis, emphasizing how algorithms and data structures affect execution time. Students examine sorting, searching, random-number generation, string matching and graph algorithms, then study computability, verification, reductions and complexity classes. Programming and mathematical exercises develop algorithmic understanding, while projects require students to design, execute and report experimental investigations of performance.
coursesExamined.discipline: Computer science; Algorithm design and analysis; Computational complexity
coursesExamined.topics: Abstract data structures; Asymptotic complexity; Random-number generation and sampling; Sorting and stability; String matching and finite automata; Sequential and binary search; Graph traversal; Shortest paths and spanning trees; Topological sorting; Computability and Turing machines; Polynomial-time verification; Reductions and complexity hierarchy
coursesExamined.methods: Asymptotic time-complexity analysis; Experimental algorithm benchmarking; Algorithm implementation and tracing; Random-number generator testing; Breadth-first and depth-first search; Graph algorithm analysis; Computational reductions

coursesExamined.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Data Science
coursesExamined.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
coursesExamined.discipline: Data science
coursesExamined.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
coursesExamined.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

coursesExamined.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
coursesExamined.name: Machine Learning
coursesExamined.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
coursesExamined.discipline: Machine learning; Statistical learning; Data science
coursesExamined.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
coursesExamined.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

coursesExamined.description2: Covers computational problems in robotics. Includes forward and inverse kinematics, motion planning, collision avoidance and robotic grasping and manipulation.
coursesExamined.name: Robotics
coursesExamined.profile: Studies computational problems in robot motion and manipulation, supported by linear algebra, calculus and geometric modelling. Students analyze forward and inverse kinematics, configuration spaces, collision-free motion planning and grasping, with shorter introductions to sensing and control. Practical work programs a robot arm and gripper; research investigates inverse kinematics for an articulated structure. A smaller component examines a chosen legal, ethical, safety or human-robot issue.
coursesExamined.discipline: Robotics; Computer science; Applied mathematics; Engineering
coursesExamined.topics: Robot architecture and industrial automation; Rotations, orientations and rigid transformations; Forward and inverse kinematics; Trajectory generation; Configuration spaces and obstacles; Exact, approximate and sampling-based motion planning; Collision detection; Sensing and control; Form and force closure; Caging; Non-prehensile manipulation; Social and ethical aspects of robotics
coursesExamined.methods: Coordinate-frame modelling of articulated structures; Analytic and iterative inverse kinematics; Mathematica computation; Configuration-space modelling; Motion-planning analysis; Collision-detection analysis; Instantaneous-motion and wrench analysis; Robot-arm and gripper programming; Modelling of physical manipulation

coursesExamined.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
coursesExamined.name: Introduction to Programming
coursesExamined.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
coursesExamined.discipline: Computer science; Programming; Discrete mathematics
coursesExamined.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
coursesExamined.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

coursesExamined.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
coursesExamined.name: Mathematical Methods
coursesExamined.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
coursesExamined.discipline: Mathematics; Calculus; Applied mathematics
coursesExamined.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
coursesExamined.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

coursesExamined.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
coursesExamined.name: Linear Algebra
coursesExamined.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
coursesExamined.discipline: Linear algebra; Applied mathematics
coursesExamined.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
coursesExamined.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

coursesExamined.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
coursesExamined.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
coursesExamined.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
coursesExamined.discipline: Numerical analysis; Computational mathematics; Scientific computing
coursesExamined.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
coursesExamined.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods

coursesExamined.description2: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.
coursesExamined.name: Advanced Calculus

coursesExamined.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
coursesExamined.name: Linear Systems
coursesExamined.profile: Analyzes continuous- and discrete-time signals and linear time-invariant systems through differential or difference equations, impulse responses and frequency-domain representations. Convolution, Fourier series and transforms lead into sampling and reconstruction, filtering, communication systems, Laplace and Z-transforms, and linear feedback. Mathematica laboratories and an applied project connect mathematical properties to signal processing and system behaviour.
coursesExamined.discipline: Applied mathematics; Signal processing; Systems and control
coursesExamined.topics: Continuous- and discrete-time signals; System linearity, causality and stability; Impulse and frequency responses; Convolution; Fourier series and transforms; Time-frequency representations; Sampling, reconstruction and aliasing; Digital filtering; Modulation and multiplexing; Laplace and Z-transforms; Regions of convergence and pole-zero representations; Linear feedback and stability
coursesExamined.methods: Convolution sums and integrals; Fourier-series and Fourier-transform analysis; Bode-plot analysis; Sampling and signal reconstruction; Filter analysis; Modulation and demodulation; Laplace and Z-transform analysis; Block-diagram system analysis; Root-locus analysis; Mathematica signal and system computation

coursesExamined.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
coursesExamined.name: Probability & Statistics
coursesExamined.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
coursesExamined.discipline: Probability theory; Mathematical statistics
coursesExamined.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
coursesExamined.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

coursesExamined.description2: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.
coursesExamined.name: Building with Nature
coursesExamined.profile: Introduces approaches that combine human infrastructure with natural processes and ecosystem health, with particular attention to Zeeland and the history of water management on Walcheren. Students examine applications across sandy and muddy coasts, lowland lakes, rivers and estuaries, cities and ports. Projects investigate ecological connectivity and formulate a Building with Nature intervention; a practical wall-building project explores constructed structures.
coursesExamined.discipline: Ecological engineering; Environmental planning; Ecology
coursesExamined.topics: Nature-based infrastructure; Coastal and water management; Walcheren's water-management history; Sandy and muddy coasts; Lowland lakes; Rivers and estuaries; Urban nature-based solutions; Harbour habitats; Habitat connectivity; Ecoducts and fish ladders
coursesExamined.methods: Building with Nature case analysis; Ecological-corridor project analysis; Nature-based intervention design; Construction and testing of model walls

coursesExamined.description2: Explores sustainable water management in delta regions. Focuses on adaptation to rising seas, floods and land subsidence; engages students in projects in Zeeland; and highlights nature‑based solutions and resilient infrastructure.
coursesExamined.name: Living with Water
coursesExamined.profile: Examines how delta societies manage water risks and opportunities, using Zeeland as a central case. Physical and ecological challenges such as flooding, salinization, freshwater scarcity, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, considering trade-offs and long-term consequences. Site-based inquiry and a project apply these concepts to context-sensitive adaptation in a delta region.
coursesExamined.discipline: Water management; Environmental governance; Delta sustainability
coursesExamined.topics: Delta environments; Flood risk and protection; Drainage and freshwater management; Sea-level rise and subsidence; Salinization; Water infrastructure and ecological consequences; Water governance, law and justice; Contaminants and pollution; EU Water Framework Directive; Nature-based adaptation; Urban ecology and water; Long-term delta resilience
coursesExamined.methods: Site-based water-management case analysis; Comparative appraisal of engineered and nature-based solutions; Context-sensitive adaptation-strategy development

coursesExamined.description2: Studies ecological processes in marine environments such as estuaries, rocky shores and coral reefs. Examines human impacts and includes guest lectures, lab visits, excursions and field work, culminating in an essay.
coursesExamined.name: Marine Biology
coursesExamined.profile: Examines marine ecological processes, ocean systems and human impacts on the sea. Physical and chemical oceanography support the study of primary and secondary production, microbial ecology, and habitats from estuaries and shores to the open ocean, deep sea and polar regions. Student seminars address fisheries, aquaculture, acidification, sea-level rise and plastic pollution. A multimedia outreach project translates a marine biological topic for a public audience.
coursesExamined.discipline: Marine biology; Marine ecology; Oceanography
coursesExamined.topics: Physical and chemical oceanography; Primary and secondary production; Marine microbial ecology; Estuaries; Rocky and sandy shores; Pelagic and continental-shelf ecosystems; Deep-sea ecosystems; Mangroves and seagrass; Coral reefs; Polar marine environments; Fisheries and aquaculture; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Marine plastic pollution
coursesExamined.methods: Multimedia marine-science communication

coursesExamined.description2: Provides hands‑on experience with GIS and data integration using geospatial data from satellites and drones. Uncovers how human actions impact ecosystems and climate and promotes sustainable practices through research projects.
coursesExamined.name: Earth Observation
coursesExamined.profile: Develops geospatial analysis for investigating environmental change and designing responses to Earth-system problems. Hands-on ArcGIS Pro work covers spatial data models, georeferencing, projections, visualization, queries, transformations and surface analysis. Remote-sensing foundations extend into spectral signatures, acquisition systems, preprocessing and image processing. A collaborative case study applies geospatial methods to an environmental research question.
coursesExamined.discipline: Geographic information science; Remote sensing; Environmental science
coursesExamined.topics: Spatial concepts and data models; Geospatial databases; Georeferencing and map projections; Spatial visualization; Spatial queries and transformations; Surface analysis; Earth-observation tools; Spectral signatures; Remote-sensing acquisition systems; Image preprocessing and processing; Environmental geospatial applications
coursesExamined.methods: ArcGIS Pro spatial analysis; Spatial-data collection and database management; Georeferencing and coordinate transformation; Geospatial visualization and queries; Surface analysis; Remote-sensing preprocessing; Image processing; Geospatial case-study design

coursesExamined.description2: Provides key concepts in physics, chemistry, materials science, mathematics and modelling necessary for sustainability. Uses a case study to connect concepts to real‑world sustainability challenges and prepares students for 200‑level sustainability courses.
coursesExamined.name: Sustainability Essentials I
coursesExamined.profile: Uses planetary boundaries to introduce scientific tools for understanding sustainability and human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and learn chemical, thermodynamic and mechanical principles relevant to environmental processes. Topics connect climate, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, energy and materials. An iterative laboratory project makes starch-based biopolymers and measures their strength and elasticity to improve the formulation.
coursesExamined.discipline: Sustainability science; Applied mathematics; Chemistry; Physics
coursesExamined.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties
coursesExamined.methods: Graph interpretation and comparison; Fermi estimation; Difference-equation and first-order linear differential-equation modelling; Elementary differentiation and integration; Biopolymer preparation; Strength and elasticity measurement; Iterative experimental improvement

coursesExamined.description2: Builds on Sustainability Essentials I. Applies tools and knowledge to a real‑world sustainability case study and allows students to delve deeper into aspects connected to their field of interest.
coursesExamined.name: Sustainability Essentials II
coursesExamined.profile: Connects wave physics, chemistry and materials science to sustainability questions. Students study wave behaviour and observation methods, chemical analysis, microscopic material structure and macroscopic stress and strain. Practical sessions include wave applications and chemistry laboratory work. Reflective inquiries and a final project critically assess sustainability campaigns, identify greenwashing and communicate evidence-based improvements to a public audience.
coursesExamined.discipline: Physics; Chemistry; Materials science; Sustainability studies
coursesExamined.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing
coursesExamined.methods: Oscilloscope wave visualization; Optical-spectroscopy interpretation; Fourier wave analysis; Copper dissolution and chemical analysis; Laboratory logbook documentation; Stress-strain analysis; Mohr's-circle application; Evidence-based greenwashing case analysis; Public sustainability-communication design

coursesExamined.description2: Teaches evaluation of environmental impacts of products, processes and services throughout their lifecycle. Emphasises strategic planning for a circular economy through hands‑on learning.
coursesExamined.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
coursesExamined.profile: Develops life-cycle approaches to evaluating products, processes and services within a circular economy. Students examine environmental, social and health consequences from resource extraction to disposal or reuse, together with costs, revenues and management strategies. Three preliminary projects develop different parts or forms of life-cycle analysis, followed by a project that integrates the stages into a full product or process assessment.
coursesExamined.discipline: Sustainability science; Industrial ecology; Life-cycle engineering and management
coursesExamined.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning
coursesExamined.methods: Life-cycle assessment; Life-cycle management strategy analysis; Environmental-impact estimation; Cost and revenue analysis; Integrated product or process assessment

coursesExamined.description2: Introduces renewable energy resources and technologies, discussing environmental, political and economic constraints. Covers energy storage and demand management and aims to balance energy supply and demand.
coursesExamined.name: Energy & Sustainability
coursesExamined.profile: Studies renewable-energy resources, conversion technologies and their integration into sustainable energy systems. Solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and biomass resources are evaluated through physical principles, resource availability and generation potential. Storage, electricity grids and demand management connect individual technologies to system reliability. Quantitative exercises, a Polysun workshop, short experiments and local mini-grid work develop the ability to assess energy options in practical environmental and economic contexts.
coursesExamined.discipline: Energy engineering; Renewable-energy systems; Sustainability science; Applied physics
coursesExamined.topics: Energy demand and renewable resources; Solar radiation and energy yield; Solar thermal and photovoltaic generation; Wind energy; Hydropower; Geothermal energy; Biomass, biogas and biofuels; Electricity grids; Energy storage; Batteries and pumped storage; Smart grids and system integration; Demand management; Mini-grids; Energy-system environmental and economic constraints
coursesExamined.methods: Renewable-energy resource and yield calculations; Polysun energy-system modelling; Hydropower sizing; Laboratory experimentation on renewable-energy systems; Energy-storage comparison; Mini-grid analysis and design

coursesExamined.description2: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.
coursesExamined.name: Renewable System Design

coursesExamined.description2: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor
coursesExamined.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
coursesExamined.profile: Provides a research-project setting for sustainability questions supplied by organizations and companies in the Zeeland delta. Small teams work with an external advisor to review literature, formulate a research question, plan and execute an investigation, and develop a final product, design or report. The substantive topic and practical techniques depend on the partner project; the common focus is an evidence-based research process and engagement with external stakeholders.
coursesExamined.discipline: Sustainability research
coursesExamined.topics: Regionally situated sustainability problems; Research-question development; Research planning; Academic literature and evidence; External stakeholder collaboration; Applied sustainability investigation
coursesExamined.methods: Literature review; Research design
